[{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Technical Tutorial: Database Replication Topologies (Leader-Follower and Multi-Leader)"},{"order":2,"type":"paragraph","text":"Replication involves copying data from one database server to multiple machines. It provides fault tolerance, improves read scalability, and reduces latency for globally distributed users. Choosing the correct replication topology is a foundational decision in system architecture."},{"order":3,"type":"subheading","text":"1. Leader-Follower (Master-Slave) Replication"},{"order":4,"type":"paragraph","text":"In a Leader-Follower topology, one node is designated as the leader (or master) and all other connected nodes are followers (or read replicas or slaves). Writes are strictly sent to the leader, which applies the change locally and sends a stream of data changes to the followers."},{"order":5,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Leader Node: Handles all write operations (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE) and optionally reads."},{"order":6,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Follower Nodes: Receive write logs from the leader and handle read operations to scale read throughput."},{"order":7,"type":"subheading","text":"Synchronous vs. Asynchronous Replication"},{"order":8,"type":"paragraph","text":"The consistency and availability trade-off in leader-follower setups depends heavily on how propagation is handled:"},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Synchronous: The leader waits for acknowledgement from followers before confirming a transaction to the client. Guarantees consistency, but degrades write performance and availability if a follower fails."},{"order":10,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Asynchronous: The leader commits the write locally and responds immediately, propagating changes in the background. High write performance, but risks data loss during leader failures (replication lag)."},{"order":11,"type":"subheading","text":"2. Multi-Leader (Master-Master) Replication"},{"order":12,"type":"paragraph","text":"When an application requires writes to be accepted in multiple data centers or regions, a single leader becomes a bottleneck and a single point of failure. Multi-leader replication allows more than one node to accept writes. Each leader acts as both a leader for local clients and a follower for other leaders."},{"order":13,"type":"subheading","text":"Handling Write Conflicts in Multi-Leader Topologies"},{"order":14,"type":"paragraph","text":"The primary challenge of multi-leader replication is write conflicts. If two users modify the same record concurrently in two different data centers, their writes will diverge and require conflict resolution."},{"order":15,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Last Write Wins (LWW): Attach timestamps and discard older updates. Prone to data loss due to clock skew."},{"order":16,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Merge Logic: Programmatically merge conflicting values (e.g., combining items in a shopping cart)."},{"order":17,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs): Specialized data structures that automatically resolve concurrent updates mathematically."},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"Code Example: Configuring Replication Parameters"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"Below is a conceptual configuration example for setting up a PostgreSQL follower node via recovery settings."},{"order":20,"type":"code","text":"# Inside postgresql.conf on the follower node
hot_standby = on

# Inside standby.signal (empty file required in PostgreSQL 12+)
# Inside primary_conninfo inside postgresql.conf
primary_conninfo = 'host=192.168.1.100 port=5432 user=replicator password=secret_pass sslmode=prefer'"},{"order":21,"type":"subheading","text":"Summary"},{"order":22,"type":"paragraph","text":"Use Leader-Follower configurations for standard applications needing read scaling and simple high availability. Use Multi-Leader configurations for multi-datacenter setups, offline operation capabilities, and collaborative tools, while carefully planning your conflict resolution strategy."}]
